article.overview: A neutral atom analyser is a scientific instrument that detects neutral atoms, which are particles with no net electric charge, leaving a planetary surface, and measures their energy, arrival direction and, where possible, mass. On airless bodies such as the Moon, some solar wind ions striking the surface are reflected back into space as energetic neutral atoms (ENAs), so these measurements provide a way to study how the solar wind interacts with the surface and with local magnetic fields [4][1]. This article covers two documented, flown examples: the Sub-keV Atom Reflecting Analyzer (SARA) on India's Chandrayaan-1 mission, which observed from orbit [4][5], and the Advanced Small Analyzer for Neutrals (ASAN) on China's Chang'E-4 Yutu-2 rover, which measures from the surface [1][2][3]. The payload name describes a class of instrument rather than one standard design, so the numerical values below apply only to the named examples.
article.description: A neutral atom analyser must first make a neutral particle measurable. Neutral atoms are not deflected by electric fields, so the instrument typically passes them over a conversion surface that ionises them, and then sorts the resulting ions by energy and by mass using electrostatic and time-of-flight sections [3]. Some instruments also carry a separate solar wind ion monitor, so that the incoming ion flux can be compared with the reflected atoms. SARA, for example, combined a neutral atom sensor (CENA) with a solar wind monitor (SWIM) and a common digital processing unit [4][5]. A neutral atom analyser is different from a neutral gas mass spectrometer, which measures the composition of thermal gas in an exosphere. That is a different instrument class and is outside the scope of this article.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purpose is to observe the interaction between the solar wind and the surface. Measurements of reflected ENAs show how much of the incoming solar wind is returned rather than absorbed, which tests assumptions about the surface and its plasma environment [4]. The SARA science objectives listed by ISRO were imaging surface composition, including permanently shadowed and volatile-rich areas; imaging the interaction between the solar wind and the surface; and imaging magnetic anomalies on the lunar surface [5]. ASAN measures the direction-, energy- and mass-resolved ENA flux at the surface, which supports study of solar wind–surface interaction and local magnetic anomaly effects, and its authors discuss the implications for the near-surface plasma environment [2]. The sources reviewed list these as objectives or interpretations; they do not present quantified results for the volatile or composition objectives.
article.operating_principle: Solar wind ions that strike the surface can be reflected as neutral atoms. An analyser detects these neutrals and converts them to measurable ions. The ASAN design deflects incoming neutral particles, ionises them on a diamond-like carbon conversion surface, and then sorts them by energy and mass-to-charge using an electrostatic analyser and a time-of-flight section [3]. This allows the instrument to separate neutral hydrogen, helium and oxygen-group atoms, with a mass resolution of about 2 [3]. The SARA CENA sensor is an energetic neutral atom imaging mass analyser that measured neutral atoms from orbit [4]. The internal mechanism of CENA is not described in detail in the sources reviewed for this article.
article.scientific_importance: Before in-situ measurement, reflected-particle observations of the Moon came from orbit. SARA's observations on Chandrayaan-1 found that about 20% of incident solar wind ions are backscattered from the lunar surface as ENAs, which contradicted the earlier assumption that the surface absorbs almost all of the solar wind [4]. The authors note that the result may also apply to other airless bodies in the solar system [4]. ASAN was the first instrument to measure energetic neutral atoms directly on the lunar surface, which made it possible to study the reflected-particle environment at the surface rather than only from orbit [2][3]. The two examples therefore provide complementary orbital and surface observations, but they belong to separate missions and should not be treated as one dataset.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal mass, size or power value for a neutral atom analyser. The values below are given for each named instrument and source. Where sources disagree, both values are stated.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No verified external dimensions were obtained for either example in this run. The sources reviewed give masses and component roles but not enclosure dimensions. A new neutral atom analyser would need its dimensions set by its field of view, energy range, mass resolution and mounting constraints, rather than by reference to the examples above.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: ASAN: 0.97 kg including electronics, per the library catalogue record of the 2020 paper [3]. SARA: 4.5 kg total as rounded on the ISRO page, with CENA 2 kg, SWIM 0.5 kg and DPU 2 kg [5]. A search excerpt gave 4.4 kg for SARA, which is unverified. The two examples differ in architecture and should not be compared as like-for-like designs.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: ASAN: 3.4 W, per the library catalogue record of the 2020 paper [3]. SARA: not stated on the ISRO page [5]; an unverified search excerpt gave 17.1 W [4]. No power figure is asserted for a new instrument.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A neutral atom analyser must function in vacuum and withstand the large temperature changes of the lunar surface, while also being exposed to radiation and micrometeoroid impacts. ASAN has been operated periodically on the surface, and its rover mobility has been used to vary the observation direction [2]. The sources reviewed do not publish thermal, radiation or vibration qualification limits for either example, so these requirements are not quantified in this article. SARA observed the surface from orbit [2][4], which imposes different environmental and geometric conditions from a surface instrument.
article.limitations: An analyser samples arriving atoms through a limited field of view. ASAN's single angular pixel covers 37 degrees by 30 degrees [3], so it samples one direction at a time and must be pointed, here by the rover, to build up a directional picture [2]. Its energy resolution is typically about 30% [3], and its mass resolution of about 2 separates only broad groups of elements [3]. The sources do not report measured accuracy or detection limits for either example. The ASAN mass and power values come from a bibliographic record rather than the full paper, and the SARA mass and power figures conflict across sources.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: Neutral atom analysers have flown in two configurations among the documented examples: as a surface instrument on a lunar rover (ASAN) and as an orbiter payload (SARA). The sources reviewed do not describe the full transportation chain for either example.
transportation_process: ASAN: installed on the Yutu-2 rover of the Chang'E-4 mission, which began operations in January 2019 [2]. Earth integration, launch, lunar transfer and landing steps were not verified and are not described.
SARA: flown as an orbiter payload on Chandrayaan-1 [4][5]. Integration, orbit insertion and commissioning details were not verified in this run.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: ASAN is a rover-mounted surface instrument whose viewing direction is changed by rover mobility [2]. SARA is an orbiter-mounted instrument with no deployment mechanism described in the sources reviewed [5]. No deployment mechanism is asserted for a new instrument.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Chandrayaan-1 SARA (orbital, flown) and Chang'E-4 ASAN (surface, flown on Yutu-2) are the two examples documented in this article.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No lander, rover or spacecraft compatibility is asserted for any example, because verified interface evidence was not obtained. The EPSC 2024 abstract places the ASAN landing site at the edge of a large magnetic anomaly in the South Pole–Aitken basin [2]; this describes the site and is not a recommendation.

article.historical_significance: SARA's observations challenged the assumption that the lunar surface absorbs nearly all of the incoming solar wind, by showing that about 20% of incident solar wind ions are returned as ENAs [4]. ASAN became the first instrument to measure energetic neutral atoms directly on the lunar surface, and its surface operations have since been reviewed over a five-year period [2][3].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The payload name "neutral atom analyser" describes a class of instrument, not one design, and the examples in this article are not interchangeable. The ASAN mass and power values (970 g and 3.4 W) and the 3 s spectrum time come from a library catalogue record of the 2020 Space Science Reviews paper [3], which was the only accessible source for those numbers. A secondary summary gives 4 s for the spectrum time, and this remains unresolved. SARA's energy range conflicts across sources (10 eV to 3.2 keV on the ISRO page [5]; 10 eV to 3 keV in a search excerpt), and its total mass and power conflict (4.5 kg on the ISRO page [5]; 4.4 kg and 17.1 W in an unverified search excerpt of the arXiv paper [4]). The current operating status of ASAN and Yutu-2 was not verified. No direct image asset URLs were verified, so this article contains no images. The article does not cover neutral gas mass spectrometers, which are a different instrument class, and it does not replace the separate entry for Payload 122, Energetic neutral atom analyser.

data_quality_notes: Mass and power values for ASAN (970 g; 3.4 W) and its 3 s spectrum time are taken from a library catalogue record of the 2020 Space Science Reviews paper, not from the full text, which was not accessible.
ASAN spectrum time conflicts: 3 s in the catalogue record, 4 s in a secondary summary. Unresolved.
SARA energy range conflicts: 10 eV to 3.2 keV (ISRO page) versus 10 eV to 3 keV (search excerpt for CENA). Unresolved.
SARA total mass and power conflict: 4.5 kg (ISRO, rounded) versus 4.4 kg and 17.1 W (search excerpt of arXiv:1012.1527). The arXiv PDF could not be parsed, so the search excerpt is unverified.
The Springer full text and the IRF news item for ASAN could not be accessed; ADS returned HTTP 405 and an access-denied page was returned by a catalogue mirror.
Current operating status of Yutu-2 and ASAN was not verified. Secondary sources disagree.
No image assets were verified from official pages; image arrays are empty by design.
The generic payload name covers a class of instrument. The examples are not interchangeable, and the SARA and ASAN numbers must not be merged.
